translations.literal: Later, at Liu Yu’s victory of Zuoli, Meng was taken alive and sent to Yan’s youngest son Hun; Hun gouged out Meng’s liver and ate it raw.
translations.idiomatic: Later Liu Yu’s victory at Zuoli captured Zhang Meng alive and sent him to Yan’s youngest son Hun, who cut out his liver and devoured it raw.

sentences.zh: 詔以琰父子隕于君親，忠孝萃於一門，贈琰侍中、司空，諡曰忠肅。

translations.literal: An edict said that because Yan and his sons had perished in service to lord and kin, loyalty and filial piety were gathered in one gate; Yan was posthumously awarded Palace Attendant and Minister of Works with the posthumous title “Zhongsu” (Loyal and Solemn).
translations.idiomatic: The court ruled that Yan and his sons had died for sovereign and family alike, blending loyalty and filial piety; Yan was posthumously named palace attendant and minister of works with the epithet Zhongsu, ‘Loyal and Stern.’

sentences.zh: 三子：肇、峻、混。

translations.literal: Three sons: Zhao, Jun, and Hun.
translations.idiomatic: He had three sons: Zhao, Jun, and Hun.

sentences.zh: 肇曆驃騎參軍，峻以琰勳封建昌侯。

translations.literal: Zhao had served as aide to the General of Agile Cavalry; Jun by Yan’s merit was enfeoffed as Marquis of Jianchang.
translations.idiomatic: Zhao had been on the staff of the general of agile cavalry; Jun held the Jianchang marquisate earned by Yan’s merit.

sentences.zh: 及沒於賊，詔贈肇散騎常侍，峻散騎侍郎。

translations.literal: When they fell among the bandits, an edict posthumously awarded Zhao Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary and Jun Cavalier Gentleman-in-Attendance.
translations.idiomatic: Their deaths among the rebels brought posthumous honors: Zhao as cavalier attendant and Jun as cavalier gentleman.

translations.literal: A double equals sign printed in the received text as a layout divider.

sentences.zh: 琰子 混

translations.literal: Yan’s son: Hun.
translations.idiomatic: Yan’s son: Hun

sentences.zh: 混字叔源。

translations.literal: Hun, courtesy name Shuyuan.
translations.idiomatic: Hun’s courtesy name was Shuyuan.

sentences.zh: 少有美譽，善屬文。

translations.literal: In youth he had a fine reputation and was adept at composing texts.
translations.idiomatic: Young Hun was celebrated and wrote superb prose.

sentences.zh: 初，孝武帝為晉陵公主求婿，謂王珣曰：「主婿但如劉真長、王子敬便足。

translations.literal: Earlier, Emperor Xiaowu sought a son-in-law for the Princess of Jinling and said to Wang Xun: “The princess’s husband need only be like Liu Tan and Wang Zijing and that would suffice.”
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu once sought a husband for the Jinling princess and told Wang Xun, ‘Someone in the mold of Liu Tan or Wang Xianzhi would do.’

sentences.zh: 如王處仲、桓元子誠可，才小富貴，便豫人家事。

translations.literal: “Men like Wang Dun and Huan Wen are certainly acceptable, but once they have a little wealth and rank they meddle in others’ affairs.”
translations.idiomatic: ‘Figures such as Wang Dun or Huan Wen have talent, yet the moment they grow rich and powerful they meddle where they should not.’

sentences.zh: 」珣對曰：「謝混雖不及真長，不減子敬。

translations.literal: Xun replied: “Though Xie Hun does not match Zhenchang, he is not inferior to Zijing.”
translations.idiomatic: Xun answered, ‘Xie Hun may fall short of Liu Tan, but he is every bit Wang Xianzhi’s peer.’

sentences.zh: 」帝曰：「如此便足。

translations.literal: The emperor said: “If so, that suffices.”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, ‘Then he will do.’

sentences.zh: 」未幾，帝崩，袁山松欲以女妻之，珣曰：「卿莫近禁臠。

translations.literal: Before long the emperor died; Yuan Shansong wished to give Hun his daughter as wife; Xun said: “You must not approach the forbidden cut of meat.”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor died soon after. When Yuan Shansong wanted Hun for his daughter, Xun warned, ‘Stay away from the emperor’s reserved dish.’

sentences.zh: 」初，元帝始鎮建業，公私窘罄，每得一㹠，以為珍膳，項上一臠尤美，輒以薦帝，群下未嘗敢食，于時呼為「禁臠」，故珣因以為戲。

translations.literal: Earlier, when Emperor Yuan first garrisoned Jianye, public and private were destitute; whenever they obtained a pig, they regarded it as a rare dish, and the cut from the nape was especially fine—always they presented it to the emperor, and those below never dared to eat; at that time it was called the “forbidden cut,” so Xun used it in jest.
translations.idiomatic: The joke referred to old Jianye days when pork was scarce and the best morsel went straight to the throne—‘forbidden cut’—so courtiers likened the prized Hun to that delicacy.

sentences.zh: 混竟尚主，襲父爵。

translations.literal: Hun in the end married the princess and inherited his father’s noble rank.
translations.idiomatic: Hun married the princess and inherited Yan’s title.

sentences.zh: 桓玄嘗欲以安宅為營，混曰：「召伯之仁，猶惠及甘棠；

translations.literal: Huan Xuan once wished to take An’s house for a barracks; Hun said: “The Duke of Shao’s benevolence still extended to the sweet pear trees;
translations.idiomatic: Huan Xuan wanted to seize An’s house for barracks; Hun protested, ‘The Duke of Shao’s kindness lingered in the pear trees—

sentences.zh: 文靖之德，更不保五畝之宅邪？

translations.literal: could Wenjing’s virtue not even protect a five-mu homestead?”
translations.idiomatic: could Wenjing’s memory not shelter five mu of roof?’

sentences.zh: 」玄聞，慚而止。

translations.literal: Xuan heard, felt shame, and desisted.
translations.idiomatic: Ashamed, Huan Xuan dropped the plan.

sentences.zh: 歷中書令、中領軍、尚書左僕射、領選。

translations.literal: He successively served as Palace Secretariat Director, Central Supervising General, Left Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and head of selection.
translations.idiomatic: He served as director of the palace secretariat, central supervising general, left vice director, and chief of personnel selection.

sentences.zh: 以党劉毅誅，國除。

translations.literal: He was executed for affiliating with Liu Yi, and the state was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: His tie to Liu Yi cost him his life and his fief.

sentences.zh: 及宋受禪，謝晦謂劉裕曰：「陛下應天受命，登壇日恨不得謝益壽奉璽紱。

translations.literal: When Song received the abdication, Xie Huo said to Liu Yu: “When Your Majesty answered Heaven and received the mandate, on the day you ascended the altar I regretted that Xie Yishou could not bear the seal-cord.”
translations.idiomatic: At the Jin–Song transition Xie Huo told Liu Yu, ‘When you took the mandate I wished Xie Yishou could have carried the jade seal.’

sentences.zh: 」裕亦歎曰：「吾甚恨之，使後生不得見其風流！

translations.literal: Yu also sighed: “I deeply regret it—it means the younger generation cannot see his bearing!”
translations.idiomatic: Liu Yu sighed, ‘I regret it too—the young will never see his grace.’

sentences.zh: 」益壽，混小字也。

translations.literal: Yishou was Hun’s childhood name.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Yishou’ was the familiar byname of Xie Hun.

sentences.zh: 安兄 奕

translations.literal: An’s elder brother: Yi
translations.idiomatic: Xie An’s elder brother: Yi

sentences.zh: 奕字無奕，少有名譽。

translations.literal: Yi, courtesy name Wuyi, from youth had reputation.
translations.idiomatic: Yi, courtesy name Wuyi, was known early.

sentences.zh: 初為剡令，有老人犯法，奕以醇酒飲之，醉猶未已。

translations.literal: At first he was magistrate of Shàn; an old man broke the law; Yi made him drink strong wine until drunk and still did not stop.
translations.idiomatic: As magistrate of Shan he punished an elderly offender by forcing cup after cup of strong wine on him.

sentences.zh: 安時年七八歲，在奕膝邊，諫止之。

translations.literal: An at the time was seven or eight, at Yi’s knee, and remonstrated to stop him.
translations.idiomatic: An, only seven or eight, sat on his knee and begged him to stop.

sentences.zh: 奕為改容，遣之。

translations.literal: Yi thereupon changed expression and sent the man away.
translations.idiomatic: Yi checked himself and released the old man.

sentences.zh: 與桓溫善。

translations.literal: He was on good terms with Huan Wen.
translations.idiomatic: He and Huan Wen were close.

sentences.zh: 溫辟為安西司馬，猶推布衣好。

translations.literal: Wen summoned him as Marshal of the West, still esteeming their commoner friendship.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen named him marshal of the west while treating him as an old friend.

sentences.zh: 在溫坐，岸幘笑詠，無異常日。

translations.literal: In Wen’s presence he wore his cap pushed back and laughed and chanted, no different from ordinary days.
translations.idiomatic: In Huan Wen’s hall he tipped back his cap, joked, and recited poetry as casually as at home.

sentences.zh: 桓溫曰：「我方外司馬。

translations.literal: Huan Wen said: “I have an unbound marshal beyond the norms.”
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen called him ‘my unbuttoned field marshal.’

sentences.zh: 」奕每因酒，無復朝廷禮，嘗逼溫飲，溫走入南康主門避之。

translations.literal: Yi always on wine ceased observing court etiquette; he once pressed Wen to drink; Wen ran into the Princess of Nankang’s gate to avoid him.
translations.idiomatic: Drunk, Yi ignored protocol—once he chased Huan Wen with a wine cup until Wen fled through the princess of Nankang’s gate.

sentences.zh: 主曰：「君若無狂司馬，我何由得相見！

translations.literal: The princess said: “If you did not have your mad marshal, how would I have gotten to see you!”
translations.idiomatic: She laughed, ‘Without your wild marshal I would never see you here!’

sentences.zh: 」奕遂攜酒就聽事，引溫一兵帥共飲，曰：「失一老兵，得一老兵，亦何所怪。

translations.literal: Yi then carried wine to the main hall and, dragging in one of Wen’s troop commanders to drink together, said: “Lose one old soldier, gain one old soldier—what is strange in that?”
translations.idiomatic: Yi marched into her reception hall, dragged one of Huan Wen’s officers into the party, and said, ‘Trade one veteran for another—what of it?’

sentences.zh: 」溫不之責。

translations.literal: Wen did not blame him.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen let it pass.

sentences.zh: 從兄尚有德政，既卒，為西蕃所思，朝議以奕立行有素，必能嗣尚事，乃遷都督豫司冀並四州軍事、安西將軍、豫州刺史、假節。

translations.literal: His cousin Shang had benign administration; after he died, the western marches missed him; court debate held that Yi’s conduct had long been consistent, and he was sure to be able to continue Shang’s work; he was therefore promoted to command military affairs in Yu, Si, Ji, and Bing four provinces, General Who Guards the West, Governor of Yuzhou, with credential staff.
translations.idiomatic: When cousin Shang died, the west missed his rule; the court, trusting Yi’s steady character, gave him Shang’s old brief—four provinces, General Who Guards the West, Yuzhou governor, with the staff.

sentences.zh: 未幾。

translations.literal: Before long.
translations.idiomatic: Soon.

sentences.zh: 卒官，贈鎮西將軍。

translations.literal: He died in office and was posthumously awarded General Who Guards the West.
translations.idiomatic: He died in post and was posthumously named General Who Guards the West.

sentences.zh: 三子：泉、靖、玄。

translations.literal: Three sons: Quan, Jing, and Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: His three sons were Quan, Jing, and Xuan.

sentences.zh: 泉早有名譽，曆義興太守。

translations.literal: Quan early had reputation and served as Prefect of Yixing.
translations.idiomatic: Quan won early fame and became prefect of Yixing.

sentences.zh: 靖官至太常。

translations.literal: Jing’s office reached Minister of the Imperial Clan.
translations.idiomatic: Jing rose to minister of the imperial clan.

sentences.zh: =奕子 玄=

translations.literal: Equals signs framing the subheading ‘Yi’s son: Xuan’ in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: Yi’s son: Xie Xuan

sentences.zh: 玄字幼度。

translations.literal: Xuan, courtesy name Youdu.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan’s courtesy name was Youdu.

sentences.zh: 少穎悟，與從兄朗俱為叔父安所器重。

translations.literal: In youth he was quick to comprehend; together with his cousin Lang he was both valued by his uncle An.
translations.idiomatic: Bright as a boy, he and cousin Lang were favorites of their uncle An.

sentences.zh: 安嘗戒約子侄，因曰：「子弟亦何豫人事，而正欲使其佳？

translations.literal: An once admonished his sons and nephews and thereupon said: “What have young kinsmen to do with others’ affairs, yet we just wish to make them excellent?”
translations.idiomatic: An once lectured his nephews: ‘What business of the world is it how we raise our boys—except that we want them to turn out well?’

sentences.zh: 」諸人莫有言者。

translations.literal: None of those present had anything to say.
translations.idiomatic: No one answered.

sentences.zh: 玄答曰：「譬如芝蘭玉樹，欲使其生於庭階耳。

translations.literal: Xuan replied: “It is like wishing orchids and jade trees to grow in the courtyard steps.”
translations.idiomatic: Xuan said, ‘Think of orchids and jade trees—we only want them rooted on our own terrace.’

sentences.zh: 」安悅。

translations.literal: An was pleased.
translations.idiomatic: An beamed.

sentences.zh: 玄少好佩紫羅香囊，安患之，而不欲傷其意，因戲賭取，即焚之，於此遂止。

translations.literal: In youth Xuan liked to wear a purple silk sachet of incense; An worried over it but did not wish to wound his feelings; therefore in jest he wagered for it and took it, then burned it; from this [the habit] ceased.
translations.idiomatic: As a boy Xuan loved a purple incense pouch; An disapproved yet hated to scold him, so he won it in a mock wager and burned it—ending the fad.

sentences.zh: 及長，有經國才略，屢辟不起。

translations.literal: When grown, he had talent and strategy to order the state; repeatedly summoned, he did not rise.
translations.idiomatic: Grown, he showed statesmanlike gifts but spurned every summons.

sentences.zh: 後與王珣俱被桓溫辟為掾，並禮重之。

translations.literal: Later he and Wang Xun were together summoned by Huan Wen as clerks, and both were treated with ritual respect.
translations.idiomatic: He and Wang Xun later joined Huan Wen’s staff on equal honor.

sentences.zh: 轉征西將軍桓豁司馬、領南郡相、監北征諸軍事。

translations.literal: He was transferred to be Marshal to Huan Huo, General Who Conquers the West, concurrently Chancellor of Nan commandery, and overseer of northern expedition military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: He became marshal to Huan Huo, general who conquers the west, with Nan commandery and oversight of the northern campaigns.

sentences.zh: 于時苻堅強盛，邊境數被侵寇，朝廷求文武良將可以鎮禦北方者，安乃以玄應舉。

translations.literal: At that time Fu Jian was strong; the frontier was repeatedly raided; the court sought civil and military commanders of quality who could guard the north; An thereupon nominated Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: With Fu Jian pressing the border, the court wanted a northern shield; An put forward Xuan’s name.

sentences.zh: 中書郎郗超雖素與玄不善，聞而歎之，曰：「安違眾舉親，明也。

translations.literal: Though Palace Secretary Xi Chao had never been on good terms with Xuan, hearing this he sighed and said: “An goes against the crowd to elevate a kinsman—clear sightedness.”
translations.idiomatic: Xi Chao, no friend of Xuan’s, still marveled: ‘An defies the pack to lift a relative—that is clarity.’

sentences.zh: 玄必不負舉，才也。

translations.literal: “Xuan is sure not to betray the nomination—talent.”
translations.idiomatic: ‘And Xuan will prove worthy—that is judgment.’

sentences.zh: 」時咸以為不然。

translations.literal: At the time all thought otherwise.
translations.idiomatic: Everyone else scoffed.

sentences.zh: 超曰：「吾嘗與玄共在桓公府，見其使才，雖履屐間亦得其任，所以知之。

translations.literal: Chao said: “I once shared Duke Huan’s office with Xuan and saw how he employed men—even in the choice of shoe-wearers he matched the right man to the task; that is how I know.”
translations.idiomatic: Chao added, ‘I served with him under Huan Wen; he placed every man, even grooms, exactly right.’

sentences.zh: 」於是征還，拜建武將軍、兗州刺史、領廣陵相、監江北諸軍事。

translations.literal: Thereupon [Xuan] was summoned back and appointed General Who Establishes Might, Governor of Yanzhou, concurrently Chancellor of Guangling, and overseer of military affairs north of the Yangzi.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan was recalled as General Who Establishes Might, Yanzhou governor, Guangling chancellor, and commander of all forces north of the river.

sentences.zh: 時苻堅遣軍圍襄陽，車騎將軍桓沖禦之。

translations.literal: At that time Fu Jian sent troops to besiege Xiangyang; Huan Chong, General of Chariots and Cavalry, opposed them.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian besieged Xiangyang; Huan Chong rode out to meet him.

sentences.zh: 詔玄發三州人丁，遣彭城內史何謙遊軍淮泗，以為形援。

translations.literal: An edict ordered Xuan to levy men from three prefectures and sent Interior Minister of Pengcheng He Qian with a mobile column along the Huai and Si as a threatening relief.
translations.idiomatic: The court told Xuan to draft three prefectures and sent He Qian of Pengcheng to threaten Fu Jian’s flank along the Huai.

sentences.zh: 襄陽既沒，堅將彭超攻龍驤將軍戴逯于彭城。

translations.literal: After Xiangyang fell, Fu Jian’s general Peng Chao attacked Dai Lu, General Who Dragons His Banner, at Pengcheng.
translations.idiomatic: When Xiangyang collapsed, Peng Chao struck Dai Lu at Pengcheng.

sentences.zh: 玄率東莞太守高衡、後軍將軍何謙次於泗口，欲遣間使報逯，令知救至，其道無由。

translations.literal: Xuan led Gao Heng, Prefect of Dongguan, and He Qian, Rear General, to encamp at Sikou, wishing to send a secret messenger to inform Lu that rescue was coming, but no route offered itself.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan camped at Sikou with Gao Heng and He Qian, desperate to word Dai Lu that help was near yet unable to pierce the lines.

sentences.zh: 小將田泓請行，乃沒水潛行，將趣城，為賊所獲。

translations.literal: A junior officer, Tian Hong, volunteered; he submerged and swam toward the city but was taken by the enemy.
translations.idiomatic: Tian Hong swam underwater toward the city and was captured.

sentences.zh: 賊厚賂泓，使云「南軍已敗」。

translations.literal: The enemy richly bribed Hong, ordering him to say ‘The southern army has already been defeated.’
translations.idiomatic: The besiegers bought him, demanding he cry that the south had lost.

sentences.zh: 泓偽許之。

translations.literal: Hong falsely promised.
translations.idiomatic: Hong pretended to agree.

sentences.zh: 既而告城中曰：「南軍垂至，我單行來報，為賊所得，勉之！

translations.literal: Presently he told those in the city: “The southern host is almost here; I came alone to report but was seized by the bandits—hold fast!”
translations.idiomatic: At the wall he shouted that relief was hours away and urged them to stand firm.

sentences.zh: 」遂遇害。

translations.literal: Thereupon he was killed.
translations.idiomatic: They executed him.

sentences.zh: 時彭超置輜重於留城，玄乃揚聲遣謙等向留城。

translations.literal: At that time Peng Chao had parked his baggage train at Liucheng; Xuan therefore spread word that He Qian and others were marching on Liucheng.
translations.idiomatic: Peng Chao had parked supplies at Liucheng; Xuan leaked a feint toward that depot.

sentences.zh: 超聞之，還保輜重。

translations.literal: When Chao heard, he returned to guard the baggage.
translations.idiomatic: Chao wheeled back to protect his trains.

sentences.zh: 謙馳進，解彭城圍。

translations.literal: Qian galloped forward and lifted the siege of Pengcheng.
translations.idiomatic: He Qian raced in and broke the ring around Pengcheng.

sentences.zh: 超復進軍南侵，堅將句難、毛當自襄陽來會。

translations.literal: Chao again advanced south; Fu Jian’s generals Gou Nan and Mao Dang came from Xiangyang to join him.
translations.idiomatic: Chao pushed south again; Gou Nan and Mao Dang marched down from Xiangyang to reinforce him.

sentences.zh: 超圍幽州刺史田洛于三阿，有眾六萬。

translations.literal: Chao besieged Tian Luo, Governor of Youzhou, at San’a with sixty thousand men.
translations.idiomatic: Sixty thousand rebels penned Tian Luo at San’a.

sentences.zh: 詔征虜將軍謝石率水軍次塗中，右衛將軍毛安之、遊擊將軍河間王曇之、淮南太守楊廣、宣城內史丘准次堂邑。

translations.literal: An edict ordered Xie Yan, General Who Conquers the Barbarians, to lead a water force to Tu; Mao Anzhi, General of the Right Guard, Tan Zhi, Prince of Hejian and mobile general, Yang Guang, Prefect of Huainan, and Qiu Zhun, Interior Minister of Xuancheng, halted at Tangyi.
translations.idiomatic: The court sent Xie Yan’s flotilla to Tu while Mao Anzhi, Prince Tan, Yang Guang, and Qiu Zhun stacked at Tangyi.

sentences.zh: 既而盱眙城陷，高密內史毛藻沒，安之等軍人相驚，遂各散退，朝廷震動。

translations.literal: Presently Xuyi city fell; Mao Zao, Interior Minister of Gaomi, was lost; Anzhi’s troops panicked among themselves and scattered in retreat; the court was shaken.
translations.idiomatic: Xuyi fell, Mao Zao died, and Mao Anzhi’s men routed themselves, rattling the capital.

sentences.zh: 玄於是自廣陵西討難等。

translations.literal: Xuan thereupon marched west from Guangling against Gou Nan and the others.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan swung west from Guangling to strike Gou Nan’s host.

sentences.zh: 何謙解田洛圍，進據白馬，與賊大戰，破之，斬其偽將都顏。

translations.literal: He Qian relieved Tian Luo’s siege, advanced to hold Baima, fought a great battle with the enemy, routed them, and beheaded their pretender general Du Yan.
translations.idiomatic: He Qian raised the siege at San’a, seized Baima, shattered the rebels, and took Du Yan’s head.

sentences.zh: 因復進擊，又破之。

translations.literal: He thereupon pressed the attack again and again routed them.
translations.idiomatic: He pressed on and broke them a second time.

sentences.zh: 斬其偽將邵保。

translations.literal: He beheaded their pretender general Shao Bao.
translations.idiomatic: Shao Bao’s head joined Du Yan’s.

sentences.zh: 超、難引退。

translations.literal: Chao and Nan withdrew.
translations.idiomatic: Peng Chao and Gou Nan pulled back.

sentences.zh: 玄率何謙、戴逯、田洛追之，戰於君川，復大破之。

translations.literal: Xuan led He Qian, Dai Lu, and Tian Luo in pursuit, fought at Junchuan, and again smashed them.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan chased with He Qian, Dai Lu, and Tian Luo and crushed them at Junchuan.

sentences.zh: 玄參軍劉牢之攻破浮航及白船，督護諸葛侃、單父令李都又破其運艦。

translations.literal: Xuan’s aide Liu Laozhi broke the floating bridge and white boats; supervisors Zhuge Kan and Prefect of Shanfu Li Du also smashed their supply ships.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Laozhi tore the pontoon; Zhuge Kan and Li Du of Shanfu smashed their grain barges.

sentences.zh: 難等相率北走，僅以身免。

translations.literal: Nan and the others fled north together, barely escaping with their lives.
translations.idiomatic: Gou Nan’s column fled north, lucky to live.

sentences.zh: 於是罷彭城、下邳二戍。

translations.literal: Thereupon the garrisons of Pengcheng and Xiapi were abolished.
translations.idiomatic: Pengcheng and Xiapi garrisons stood down.

sentences.zh: 詔遣殿中將軍慰勞，進號冠軍，加領徐州刺史，還于廣陵，以功封東興縣侯。

translations.literal: An edict sent a Palace Guard general to console and reward; [Xuan] was advanced in rank to Champion, additionally given the governorship of Xuzhou, returned to Guangling, and by merit enfeoffed as Marquis of Dongxing county.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor’s envoy brought word of promotion to Champion, added Xuzhou, a return to Guangling, and a Dongxing county marquisate.

sentences.zh: 及苻堅自率兵次於項城，眾號百萬，而涼州之師始達咸陽，蜀漢順流，幽并系至。

translations.literal: When Fu Jian personally led troops to Xiangcheng, his host claimed a million while Liangzhou’s army had only reached Xianyang, Ba–Shu flowed downstream, and You and Bing contingents tied up.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian halted at Xiangcheng at the head of a ‘million’ while reinforcements straggled from Liangzhou, Shu, You, and Bing.

sentences.zh: 先遣苻融、慕容暐、張蠔、苻方等至潁口，梁成、王顯等屯洛澗。

translations.literal: He first sent Fu Rong, Murong Wei, Zhang Hao, Fu Fang, and others to Yingkou; Liang Cheng and Wang Xian encamped at Luojian.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Rong, Murong Wei, Zhang Hao, and Fu Fang massed at Yingkou; Liang Cheng and Wang Xian held Luojian.

sentences.zh: 詔以玄為前鋒、都督徐兗青三州揚州之晉陵幽州之燕國諸軍事，與叔父征虜將軍石、從弟輔國將軍琰、西中郎將桓伊、龍驤將軍檀玄、建威將軍戴熙、揚武將軍陶隱等距之，眾凡八萬。

translations.literal: An edict made Xuan vanguard and commander of military affairs in Xu, Yan, and Qing three provinces and the Jinling district of Yangzhou and the Yan princedom of Youzhou; with his uncle Xie Shi, General Who Conquers the Barbarians, his cousin Xie Yan, General Who Supports the State, Huan Yi, General of the Centre of the West, Tan Xuan, General Who Dragons His Banner, Dai Xi, General Who Establishes Might, and Tao Yin, General Who Rouses Might, he opposed them—eighty thousand in all.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan took the vanguard, joined Xie Shi, Xie Yan, Huan Yi, Tan Xuan, Dai Xi, and Tao Yin—eighty thousand men under one command.

sentences.zh: 玄先遣廣陵相劉牢之五千人直指洛澗，即斬梁成及成弟雲，步騎崩潰，爭赴淮水。

translations.literal: Xuan first sent Liu Laozhi, Chancellor of Guangling, with five thousand straight at Luojian, immediately beheading Liang Cheng and Cheng’s younger brother Yun; infantry and cavalry collapsed, struggling into the Huai.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Laozhi’s five thousand hit Luojian, killed Liang Cheng and Liang Yun, and hurled Fu Jian’s van into the Huai.

sentences.zh: 牢之縱兵追之，生擒堅偽將梁他、王顯、梁悌、慕容屈氏等，收其軍實。

translations.literal: Laozhi unleashed pursuit, took alive Fu Jian’s pretender generals Liang Ta, Wang Xian, Liang Ti, Murong Qushi, and others, and seized their military stores.
translations.idiomatic: Laozhi ran them down, bagging Liang Ta, Wang Xian, Liang Ti, Murong Qushi, and their gear.

sentences.zh: 堅進屯壽陽，列陣臨肥水，玄軍不得渡。

translations.literal: Jian advanced to encamp at Shouyang, drew up battle lines along the Fei River, and Xuan’s army could not cross.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian stacked at Shouyang along the Fei, blocking Xuan’s crossing.

sentences.zh: 玄使謂苻融曰：「君遠涉吾境，而臨水為陣，是不欲速戰。

translations.literal: Xuan sent word to Fu Rong: “You have crossed far into our territory yet array yourselves along the water—you do not wish a swift battle.”
translations.idiomatic: Xuan told Fu Rong, ‘You invade yet hug the river—you shrink from a quick fight.’

sentences.zh: 諸君稍卻，令將士得周旋，僕與諸君緩轡而觀之，不亦樂乎！

translations.literal: “If you gentlemen will draw back slightly so our warriors may maneuver, I and you gentlemen may rein in our horses and watch—would that not be pleasant!”
translations.idiomatic: ‘Step back a little, let the ranks breathe, and we can watch from the saddle—far more satisfying.’

sentences.zh: 」堅眾皆曰：「宜阻肥水，莫令得上。

translations.literal: Fu Jian’s host all said: “We should block the Fei and not let them ascend.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian’s officers said, ‘Hold the Fei—never let them ford.’

sentences.zh: 我眾彼寡，勢必萬全。

translations.literal: We are many and they few; the situation is sure to be utterly safe.
translations.idiomatic: ‘We outnumber them—safety demands we hold the line.’

sentences.zh: 」堅曰：「但卻軍，令得過，而我以鐵騎數十萬向水，逼而殺之。

translations.literal: Jian said: “Only draw the army back, let them cross, and I will press several hundred thousand armored horsemen to the water’s edge and crush them.”
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian said, ‘Pull back, let them ford, then ride hundreds of thousands of armored horses to the bank and crush them.’

sentences.zh: 」融亦以為然，遂麾使卻陣，眾因亂不能止。

translations.literal: Rong also thought it right; thereupon he signaled the lines to withdraw, and the host fell into disorder and could not be stopped.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Rong agreed; the order to retreat broke the formation beyond recall.

sentences.zh: 於是玄與琰、伊等以精銳八千涉渡肥水。

translations.literal: Thereupon Xuan with Yan, Yi, and others took eight thousand picked troops across the Fei.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan, Xie Yan, and Huan Yi splashed eight thousand elites over the Fei.

sentences.zh: 石軍距張蠔，小退。

translations.literal: Shi’s army opposed Zhang Hao and gave a little ground.
translations.idiomatic: Xie Shi’s line facing Zhang Hao bent slightly.

sentences.zh: 玄、琰仍進，決戰肥水南。

translations.literal: Xuan and Yan pressed on and fought a decisive battle south of the Fei.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan and Xie Yan slammed home south of the river.

sentences.zh: 堅中流矢，臨陣斬融。

translations.literal: Jian was struck by a stray arrow; [someone] beheaded Rong in the fighting.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian took an arrow; Fu Rong died on the field.

sentences.zh: 堅眾奔潰，自相蹈藉投水死者不可勝計，肥水為之不流。

translations.literal: Jian’s host fled in rout, trampling one another and drowning in numbers beyond counting; the Fei ceased to flow.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian’s horde stampeded into the Fei until the river dammed with corpses.

sentences.zh: 餘眾棄甲宵遁，聞風聲鶴唳，皆以為王師已至，草行露宿，重以饑凍，死者十七八。

translations.literal: The remainder cast armor and fled by night; hearing wind in the trees and cranes crying, all thought the royal army had arrived; they slept in the open and starved in the cold—seven or eight in ten died.
translations.idiomatic: Survivors fled by night, mistook wind and crane calls for Jin drums, and froze or starved—eight in ten perished.

sentences.zh: 獲堅乘輿雲母車，儀服、器械、軍資、珍寶山積，牛馬驢騾駱駝十萬餘。

translations.literal: They captured Fu Jian’s imperial carriage of mica, regalia, weapons, supplies, and treasures heaped like mountains, and more than a hundred thousand head of oxen, horses, donkeys, mules, and camels.
translations.idiomatic: They took Fu Jian’s mica coach, mountains of gear, and a hundred thousand head of livestock.

sentences.zh: 詔遣殿中將軍慰勞。

translations.literal: An edict sent a Palace Guard general to console and reward.
translations.idiomatic: The throne again sent an envoy with gifts.

sentences.zh: 進號前將軍、假節，固讓不受。

translations.literal: He was advanced to Forward General with credential staff but firmly declined and did not accept.
translations.idiomatic: They offered Forward General and the staff; Xuan refused.

sentences.zh: 賜錢百萬，彩千匹。

translations.literal: He was gifted a million cash and a thousand bolts of colored silk.
translations.idiomatic: A million cash and a thousand bolts of silk followed.

sentences.zh: 既而安奏苻堅喪敗，宜乘其釁會，以玄為前鋒都督，率冠軍將軍桓石虔徑造渦潁，經略舊都。

translations.literal: Presently An submitted that, with Fu Jian broken, the moment should be seized; Xuan was made vanguard commander and led Huan Shiquan, Champion General, straight to Guo and Ying to plan recovery of the old capital.
translations.idiomatic: An urged a follow-up: Xuan led Huan Shiquan toward the Guo–Ying line to retake the ancient metropolis.

sentences.zh: 玄復率眾次於彭城，遣參軍劉襲攻堅兗州刺史張崇于鄄城，走之，使劉牢之守鄄城。

translations.literal: Xuan again brought the host to Pengcheng, sent aide Liu Xi to attack Fu Jian’s Governor of Yanzhou Zhang Chong at Juancheng and drive him off, and had Liu Laozhi hold Juancheng.
translations.idiomatic: He camped at Pengcheng, chased Zhang Chong from Juancheng, and left Liu Laozhi there.

sentences.zh: 兗州既平，玄患水道險澀，糧運艱難，用督護聞人奭謀，堰呂梁水，樹柵，立七埭為派，擁二岸之流，以利運漕，自此公私利便。

translations.literal: With Yanzhou pacified, Xuan worried that the waterway was treacherous and grain transport hard; adopting supervisor Wenren Shi’s plan, he dammed the water at Lüliang, planted palisades, raised seven diversion dikes, and choked both banks to ease transport—thereafter public and private alike benefited.
translations.idiomatic: Yanzhou won, he dammed Lüliang, threw up seven dikes, and eased logistics for everyone.

sentences.zh: 又進伐青州，故謂之青州派。

translations.literal: He also advanced against Qingzhou, hence it was called the Qingzhou diversion.
translations.idiomatic: The works became known as the Qingzhou channel.

sentences.zh: 遣淮陵太守高素以三千人向廣固，降堅青州刺史苻朗。

translations.literal: He sent Gao Su, Prefect of Huailing, with three thousand toward Guanggu and induced Fu Jian’s Governor of Qingzhou Fu Lang to surrender.
translations.idiomatic: Gao Su took three thousand men to Guanggu and won Fu Lang’s surrender.

sentences.zh: 又進伐冀州，遣龍驤將軍劉牢之、濟北太守丁匡據碻磝，濟陽太守郭滿據滑台，奮武將軍顏雄渡河立營。

translations.literal: He again advanced against Jizhou, sent Liu Laozhi, General Who Dragons His Banner, and Ding Kuang, Prefect of Jibei, to hold Qiao’ao, Guo Man, Prefect of Jiyang, to hold Hua Terrace, and Yan Xiong, General Who Rouses Might, to throw a camp across the Yellow River.
translations.idiomatic: He pushed into Jizhou: Liu Laozhi and Ding Kuang seized Qiao’ao, Guo Man took Hua Terrace, Yan Xiong bridged the Yellow River.

sentences.zh: 堅子丕遣將桑據屯黎陽。

translations.literal: Fu Jian’s son Pi sent general Sang Ju to garrison Liyang.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Pi posted Sang Ju at Liyang.

sentences.zh: 玄命劉襲夜襲據，走之。

translations.literal: Xuan ordered Liu Xi to raid Sang Ju by night and drive him off.
translations.idiomatic: Liu Xi’s night attack scattered Sang Ju.

sentences.zh: 丕惶遽欲降，玄許之。

translations.literal: Pi was terrified and wished to surrender; Xuan permitted it.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Pi begged to yield; Xuan accepted.

sentences.zh: 丕告饑，玄饋丕米二千斛。

translations.literal: Pi reported famine; Xuan sent Pi two thousand hu of rice.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan fed him two thousand hu of grain.

sentences.zh: 又遣晉陵太守滕恬之渡河守黎陽，三魏皆降。

translations.literal: He also sent Teng Tianzhi, Prefect of Jinling, across the river to hold Liyang; the three Wei regions all submitted.
translations.idiomatic: Teng Tianzhi crossed to Liyang and the heartland of Wei capitulated.

sentences.zh: 以兗、青、司、豫平，加玄都督徐、兗、青、司、冀、幽、并七州軍事。

translations.literal: With Yan, Qing, Si, and Yu pacified, Xuan was additionally made commander of military affairs in Xu, Yan, Qing, Si, Ji, You, and Bing seven provinces.
translations.idiomatic: Four provinces quiet, Xuan took command of seven.

sentences.zh: 玄上疏以方平河北，幽冀宜須總督，司州縣遠，應統豫州。

translations.literal: Xuan submitted a memorial that, with the north of the Yellow River about to be pacified, You and Ji ought to have an overall commander, while Sizhou’s counties lay far away and should fall under unified command with Yuzhou.
translations.idiomatic: He argued that pacifying Hebei required one hand on You and Ji, while distant Sizhou was better yoked to Yuzhou.

sentences.zh: 以勳封康樂縣公。

translations.literal: By merit he was enfeoffed as Duke of Kangle county.
translations.idiomatic: Merit brought the duchy of Kangle.

sentences.zh: 玄請以先封東興侯賜兄子玩，詔聽之，更封玩豫甯伯。

translations.literal: Xuan asked that his former marquisate of Dongxing be given to his elder brother’s son Wan; an edict assented and re-enfeoffed Wan as Baron of Yuning.
translations.idiomatic: He ceded the Dongxing marquisate to nephew Wan; the court made Wan baron of Yuning instead.

sentences.zh: 復遣甯遠將軍{夭曰}演伐申凱于魏郡，破之。

translations.literal: He again sent Tian Yan, General Who Extends Stability Far, to attack Shen Kai in Wei commandery and defeat him.
translations.idiomatic: He dispatched Tian Yan against Shen Kai in Wei commandery and broke him.

sentences.zh: 玄欲令豫州刺史硃序鎮梁國，玄住彭城，北固河上，西援洛陽，內籓朝廷。

translations.literal: Xuan wished to have Zhu Xu, Governor of Yuzhou, garrison Liang state, himself stay at Pengcheng, firm the river line to the north, aid Luoyang to the west, and screen the court within.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan wanted Zhu Xu in Liang, himself at Pengcheng, shielding the river, Luoyang, and the capital.

sentences.zh: 朝議以征役既久，宜置戍而還，使玄還鎮淮陰，序鎮壽陽。

translations.literal: Court debate held the campaigns had lasted long; garrisons should be set and the army withdrawn—Xuan was sent back to guard Huaiyin, Zhu Xu to garrison Shouyang.
translations.idiomatic: The court called for drawdown: Xuan to Huaiyin, Zhu Xu to Shouyang.

sentences.zh: 會翟遼據黎陽反，執滕恬之，又泰山太守張願舉郡叛，河北騷動，玄自以處分失所，上疏送節，盡求解所職。

translations.literal: It happened that Zhai Liao seized Liyang in revolt, captured Teng Tianzhi, and Zhang Yuan, Prefect of Taishan, raised the commandery in rebellion; Hebei seethed; Xuan considered his dispositions mistaken, submitted his staff, and asked to be stripped of all posts.
translations.idiomatic: Zhai Liao took Liyang and Teng Tianzhi; Zhang Yuan mutinied in Taishan; Xuan blamed himself and offered every seal.

sentences.zh: 詔慰勞，令且還鎮淮陰，以硃序代鎮彭城。

translations.literal: An edict consoled him and ordered him meanwhile to return to Huaiyin, Zhu Xu to replace him at Pengcheng.
translations.idiomatic: The throne soothed him, kept him at Huaiyin, and shifted Zhu Xu to Pengcheng.

sentences.zh: 玄既還，遇疾，上疏解職，詔書不許。

translations.literal: When Xuan had returned, he fell ill; he submitted a memorial resigning office; the edict did not permit.
translations.idiomatic: Back at post he sickened and begged off; the emperor refused.

sentences.zh: 玄又自陳，既不堪攝職，慮有曠廢，詔又使移鎮東陽城。

translations.literal: Xuan again stated himself that he could not sustain the burden of office, fearing neglect; an edict again had him move headquarters to Dongyang city.
translations.idiomatic: He pleaded incapacity again and was ordered to Dongyang city.

sentences.zh: 玄即路，於道疾篤，上疏曰：

translations.literal: Xuan set out; on the road his illness grew grave; he submitted a memorial saying:
translations.idiomatic: En route his condition collapsed; he drafted:

sentences.zh: 臣以常人，才不佐世，忽蒙殊遇，不復自量，遂從戎政。

translations.literal: Your subject, an ordinary man, lacks talent to aid the age; suddenly receiving extraordinary favor, I failed to measure myself and followed military affairs.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I am a common man unfit to serve, yet grace swept me into the army.’

sentences.zh: 驅馳十載，不辭鳴鏑之險，每有征事，輒請為軍鋒，由恩厚忘軀，甘死若生也。

translations.literal: For ten years I galloped without shunning the whistling of arrows; whenever there was a campaign I asked to be the army’s spearhead—because grace was deep I forgot my body, gladly facing death as if life.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Ten years at the front—always first in the charge, repaying favor with my life.’

sentences.zh: 冀有毫釐，上報榮寵。

translations.literal: Hoping for the least grain [of merit], I would repay the glory and favor.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I hoped a speck of merit might match the honor given me.’

sentences.zh: 天祚大晉，王威屢舉，實由陛下神武英斷，無思不服。

translations.literal: Heaven blesses great Jin; royal might has repeatedly triumphed—truly because Your Majesty is divinely martial and decisively wise; none who think resist submission.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Heaven favors Jin; Your Majesty’s awesomeness awes every mind.’

sentences.zh: 亡叔臣安協贊雍熙，以成天工。

translations.literal: My late uncle, your subject An, assisted in the harmonious brightness and completed Heaven’s work.
translations.idiomatic: ‘My uncle An helped perfect your harmonious reign.’

sentences.zh: 而雰霧尚翳，六合未朗，遺黎塗炭，巢窟宜除，復命臣荷戈前驅，董司戎首。

translations.literal: Yet mist still veils; the six directions are not bright; surviving people are in mud and charcoal; nests of rebels should be removed; again your subject was ordered to bear a spear in the van and oversee the martial host.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Mists linger; the people still burn; you ordered me again to lead the van.’

sentences.zh: 冀仰憑皇威，宇宙甯一，陛下致太平之化，庸臣以塵露報恩，然後從亡叔臣安退身東山，以道養壽。

translations.literal: I hoped to rely on imperial majesty so the cosmos would be at peace, Your Majesty would achieve the transformation of great peace, and your humble subject might repay grace like dust and dew; then I would follow my late uncle An in withdrawing to Eastern Mountain and nurturing longevity by the Way.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I dreamed of unifying the realm, repaying you in dust and dew, then retiring east with my uncle.’

sentences.zh: 此誠以形于文旨，達於聖聽矣。

translations.literal: This sincerity has already taken form in my writings and reached sagely hearing.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I set that hope in every memorial you read.’

sentences.zh: 臣所以區區家國，實在於此，不謂臣愆咎夙積，罪鐘中年，上延亡叔臣安、亡兄臣靖，數月之間，相系殂背，下逮稚子，尋復夭昏。

translations.literal: The reason your subject has been earnest for house and state lies truly herein; I did not expect accumulated fault from early on, punishment striking mid-life, extending upward to my late uncle An and late elder brother Jing, who within months died one after another, and downward to my young sons, who soon followed in untimely death.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I meant only to serve house and state—not to watch uncle, brother, and sons die in a single season.’

sentences.zh: 哀毒兼纏，痛百常情。

translations.literal: Grief and poison twine together; pain exceeds the ordinary feeling.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Grief poisons me beyond bearing.’

sentences.zh: 臣不勝禍酷暴集，每一慟殆弊。

translations.literal: Your subject cannot withstand cruel misfortune heaped together; each bout of mourning nearly destroys me.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Each loss nearly kills me.’

sentences.zh: 所以含哀忍悲，期之必存者，雖哲輔傾落，聖明方融，伊周嗣作，人懷自厲，猶欲申臣本志，隆國保家，故能豁其情滯，同之無心耳。

translations.literal: Therefore I hold grief and endure sorrow, hoping I might yet survive: though wise ministers have fallen, sagely clarity is still bright, successors like Yi Yin and the Duke of Zhou take office, and every man steels himself—I still wish to assert my original resolve, exalt the state and guard the family; thus I could open my pent feelings and share the mind of no-selfishness.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Yet I clung to life hoping still to serve while the court found new pillars.’

sentences.zh: 去冬奉司徒道子告括囊遠圖，逮問臣進止之宜。

translations.literal: Last winter I received Prince Daozi’s sealed letter on long-range plans and was asked about advancing or holding.
translations.idiomatic: ‘Last winter the prince asked whether to push or pause.’

sentences.zh: 臣進不達事機，以蹙境為恥，退不自揆，故欲順其宿心。

translations.literal: Your subject advancing did not grasp the opportune moment and took a cramped frontier as shame; retiring, I did not measure myself and therefore wished to follow my long-held intent.
translations.idiomatic: ‘I was ashamed to yield ground yet unwilling to cling beyond my strength.’

sentences.zh: 豈謂經略不振，自貽斯戾。

translations.literal: How could I have thought strategy would falter and I would bring this blame on myself?
translations.idiomatic: ‘I never thought our plans would stall and shame would fall on me.’

sentences.zh: 是以奉送章節，待罪有司，執徇常儀，實有愧心。

translations.literal: Therefore I respectfully hand over my seals and ribbons, awaiting punishment from the relevant offices; if the routine statutes are mechanically applied, my heart will truly feel shame.
translations.idiomatic: So I return my seals to await judgment—strict justice would shame me further.

sentences.zh: 而聖恩赦過，黷法垂宥，使抱罪之臣復得更名于所司。

translations.literal: Yet sagely grace pardons fault, indulgent law extends forgiveness, letting a guilty subject again receive appointment from the offices.
translations.idiomatic: Yet Your Majesty forgave and let me keep office despite my faults.

sentences.zh: 木石猶感，而況臣乎！

translations.literal: Even wood and stone would be moved—how much more your subject!
translations.idiomatic: Stone and wood would be grateful—how much more a man.

sentences.zh: 顧將身不良，動與釁會，謙德不著，害盈是荷，先疾既動，便至委篤，陛下體臣疢重，使還籓淮側。

translations.literal: Only my body is unwell; movement meets with calamity; modest virtue does not show; I bear the brunt of overflowing harm; once the old ailment stirred, it became desperately grave; Your Majesty, cherishing my heavy illness, had me return to my fief on the Huai.
translations.idiomatic: Illness dogs me; each step invites blame; the old sickness flared until I collapsed—so you sent me back to the Huai fief.

sentences.zh: 甫欲休兵靜眾，綏懷善撫，兼苦自療，冀日月漸瘳，繕甲俟會，思更奮迅。

translations.literal: I had just wished to rest the troops and quiet the masses, soothe and cherish with good care, while painfully treating myself, hoping day by day to improve, repair armor and await the moment, thinking to rouse myself again.
translations.idiomatic: I meant to rest the army, heal myself, refit, and wait for another chance.

sentences.zh: 而所患沈頓，有增無損。

translations.literal: Yet the illness sinks and lingers, growing worse, never better.
translations.idiomatic: Instead the malady only deepened.

sentences.zh: 今者惙惙，救命朝夕。

translations.literal: Now I am faint; my life hangs on morning and evening.
translations.idiomatic: Now I cling to life hour by hour.

sentences.zh: 臣之平日，率其常矩，加以匪懈，猶不能令政理弘宣，況今內外天隔，永不復接，寧可臥居重任，以招患慮。

translations.literal: In ordinary times your subject, following the constant rule and adding tirelessness, still could not make governance broadly proclaimed; how much more now inner and outer are sundered by Heaven, never to connect again—how could I recline in a heavy post and invite worry?
translations.idiomatic: Even in health I barely governed; cut off from court, I cannot cling to high office.

sentences.zh: 追尋前事，可為寒心。

translations.literal: Tracing former affairs, it can chill the heart.
translations.idiomatic: Looking back chills the blood.

sentences.zh: 臣之微身，復何足惜，區區血誠，憂國實深。

translations.literal: Your subject’s slight person—what is worth regretting?—yet my humble blood loyalty grieves deeply for the state.
translations.idiomatic: My life is nothing; the realm is everything.

sentences.zh: 謹遣兼長史劉濟重奉送節蓋章傳。

translations.literal: I respectfully dispatch acting chief clerk Liu Ji again to present staff, canopy, seals, and tallies.
translations.idiomatic: I send Liu Ji with every seal and baton I hold.

sentences.zh: 伏願陛下垂天地之仁，拯將絕之氣，時遣軍司鎮慰荒雜，聽臣所乞，盡醫藥消息，歸誠道門，冀神祇之佑。

translations.literal: I prostrate myself, hoping Your Majesty will extend Heaven-and-earth kindness, rescue breath about to expire, timely dispatch an army commander to calm the wild confusion, grant what I beg, give me full use of physicians and rest, return sincerity to the Way’s gate, and hope for blessing from the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: I beg a physician, leave to retire into Daoist healing, and a garrison chief to steady the chaos I leave behind.

sentences.zh: 若此而不差，修短命也。

translations.literal: If after this I do not recover, it is the shortness of fate.
translations.idiomatic: If I still die, call it Heaven’s cut.

sentences.zh: 使臣得及視息，瞻睹墳柏，以此之盡，公私真無恨矣，伏枕悲慨，不覺流涕。

translations.literal: Should your subject gain breath enough to look upon ancestral tombs, with this as my end, public and private would truly have no regret; leaning on the pillow, grief wells and tears flow unbidden.
translations.idiomatic: Let me see my family graves once more and I will die content—yet thinking of it I weep on this pillow.

sentences.zh: 詔遣高手醫一人，令自消息，又使還京口療疾。

translations.literal: An edict dispatched one skilled physician, ordering self-care, and also had him return to Jingkou to treat the illness.
translations.idiomatic: The court sent a master physician and ordered him to convalesce at Jingkou.

sentences.zh: 玄奉詔便還，病久不差，又上疏曰：「臣同生七人，凋落相繼，惟臣一己，孑然獨存。

translations.literal: Xuan, receiving the edict, returned at once; the illness long did not improve, and he again submitted a memorial: “Of seven born together with your subject, they have fallen one after another; only your subject alone remains, solitary.”
translations.idiomatic: He obeyed, saw no cure, and wrote again: ‘Six siblings are gone; I alone survive.’

sentences.zh: 在生荼酷，無如臣比。

translations.literal: Among the living none has tasted bitterness like your subject.
translations.idiomatic: No one living has suffered as I have.

sentences.zh: 所以含哀忍痛，希延視息者，欲報之德，實懷罔極，庶蒙一瘳，申其此志。

translations.literal: The reason I hold grief and endure pain, hoping to prolong breath, is the virtue I wish to repay—it truly knows no limit; I hope that if I mend once, I may declare this intent.
translations.idiomatic: I cling to life only to repay you, praying one recovery will let me finish that debt.

sentences.zh: 且臣孤遺滿目，顧之惻然，為欲極其求生之心，未能自分於灰士。

translations.literal: Moreover your subject’s orphans fill the eye; looking on them is heartbreaking; I desire to exhaust the mind that seeks their life, yet cannot part myself from dust and earth.
translations.idiomatic: Orphans surround me; I cannot abandon them to the grave.

sentences.zh: 慺慺之情，可哀可湣。

translations.literal: Earnest feeling—pitiable and compassion-worthy.
translations.idiomatic: The plea is wretched.

sentences.zh: 伏願陛下矜其所訴，霈然垂恕，不令微臣銜恨泉壤。

translations.literal: I prostrate myself, hoping Your Majesty will pity what I declare, pour out forgiveness, and not let your humble subject carry resentment to the yellow springs.
translations.idiomatic: Spare me dying embittered underground.

sentences.zh: 」表寢不報。

translations.literal: The memorial was shelved without reply.
translations.idiomatic: No answer came.

sentences.zh: 前後表疏十餘上，久之。

translations.literal: Before and after, memorials and notes exceeded ten; a long time passed.
translations.idiomatic: He sent more than ten pleas over many months.

sentences.zh: 乃轉授散騎常侍、左將軍、會稽內史。

translations.literal: Thereupon he was transferred to appointment as Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary, General of the Left, and Interior Minister of Kuaiji.
translations.idiomatic: Finally he was named cavalier attendant, general of the left, and interior minister of Kuaiji.

sentences.zh: 時吳興太守晉甯侯張玄之亦以才學顯，自吏部尚書與玄同年之郡，而玄之名亞于玄，時人稱為「南北二玄」，論者美之。

translations.literal: At that time Zhang Xuanzhi, Marquis of Jinning and Prefect of Wuxing, was also eminent for talent and learning; from Director of the Ministry of Personnel he went out to his command the same year as Xuan, yet Xuanzhi’s name stood second to Xuan; people of the time called them ‘the two Xuans, north and south’—commentators praised this.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Xuanzhi left personnel the same year as Xuan; folk dubbed them the northern and southern ‘Xuan’—both stars of their age.

sentences.zh: 玄既輿疾之郡，十三年，卒于官，時年四十六。

translations.literal: Xuan, having been carried ill to his commandery, in the thirteenth year died in office at the age of forty-six.
translations.idiomatic: He took his sickbed to Kuaiji and died there at forty-six in year thirteen.

sentences.zh: 追贈車騎將軍、開府儀同三司，諡曰獻武。

translations.literal: Posthumously he was awarded General of Chariots and Cavalry and an office ceremonially equal to the Three Excellencies, with the posthumous title ‘Xianwu’ (Presented Martial).
translations.idiomatic: The court named him general of chariots and cavalry, opentent equal to the Three Excellencies, with the epithet Xianwu.

sentences.zh: 子瑍嗣，秘書郎，早卒。

translations.literal: His son Gun succeeded; [Gun was] Palace Secretary; he died young.
translations.idiomatic: Son Gun inherited, served as palace secretary, and died young.

sentences.zh: 子靈運嗣。

translations.literal: His son Lingyun succeeded.
translations.idiomatic: Lingyun next inherited the line.

sentences.zh: 瑍少不惠，而靈運文藻豔逸，玄嘗稱曰：「我尚生瑍，瑍那得生靈運！

translations.literal: Gun from youth was not clever, yet Lingyun’s literary brilliance was dazzling; Xuan once remarked: “If even I produced Gun, how could Gun produce Lingyun!”
translations.idiomatic: Gun was dull; Lingyun’s genius dazzled—Xuan joked, ‘I barely sired Gun; how did Gun sire Lingyun?’

sentences.zh: 」永熙中，為劉裕世子左衛率。

translations.literal: In the Yongxi era he was Left Guard Leader to Liu Yu’s heir.
translations.idiomatic: Under Yongxi he led the heir’s left guard for Liu Yu.

sentences.zh: =附 何謙 戴逯=

translations.literal: Equals signs framing the supplement heading ‘He Qian; Dai Lu’ in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: Appendix: He Qian and Dai Lu

sentences.zh: 始從玄征伐者，何謙字恭子，東海人，戴逯字安丘，處士逵之弟，並驍果多權略。

translations.literal: Those who first followed Xuan on campaign: He Qian, courtesy name Gongzi, a man of Donghai; Dai Lu, courtesy name Anqiu, younger brother of the recluse Dai Kui—both were fierce, resolute, and full of stratagem.
translations.idiomatic: He Qian of Donghai and Dai Lu—brother of recluse Dai Kui—were Xuan’s earliest fighters, bold and cunning.

sentences.zh: 逵厲操東山，而逯以武勇顯。

translations.literal: Kui hardened his conduct on Eastern Mountain, while Lu showed martial valor.
translations.idiomatic: Dai Kui stayed pure on Eastern Mountain; Dai Lu won fame in arms.

sentences.zh: 謝安嘗謂逯曰：「卿兄弟志業何殊？

translations.literal: Xie An once said to Lu: “How do your brothers’ aims and undertakings differ?”
translations.idiomatic: An asked Lu, ‘How do you and your brother differ in calling?’

sentences.zh: 」逯曰：「下官不堪其憂，家兄不改其樂。

translations.literal: Lu replied: “Your inferior official cannot bear the worry; my elder brother does not alter his joy.”
translations.idiomatic: Lu answered, ‘I cannot shoulder his sorrows; he never loses his joy.’

sentences.zh: 」逯以軍功封廣信侯，位至大司農。

translations.literal: Lu by military merit was enfeoffed as Marquis of Guangxin and rose to Minister of Agriculture.
translations.idiomatic: Lu earned the Guangxin marquisate and became minister of agriculture.

sentences.zh: 安弟 萬

translations.literal: An’s younger brother: Wan.
translations.idiomatic: Xie An’s brother: Wan

sentences.zh: 萬字萬石，才器雋秀，雖器量不及安，而善自炫曜，故早有時譽。

translations.literal: Wan, courtesy name Wanshi, had outstanding talent and bearing; though his capacity did not match An’s, he was skilled at displaying himself, and therefore early won contemporary praise.
translations.idiomatic: Wan, courtesy Wanshi, flashed brilliance—less depth than An but a genius at self-promotion.

sentences.zh: 工言論，善屬文，敘漁父、屈原、季主、賈誼、楚老、龔勝、孫登、嵇康四隱四顯為《八賢論》，其旨以處者為優，出者為劣，以示孫綽。

translations.literal: He was skilled in pure talk and adept at composition; he arranged the Fisherman, Qu Yuan, Jizhu, Jia Yi, the Old Man of Chu, Gong Sheng, Sun Deng, and Xi Kang—four recluses and four in office—as the ‘Treatise on the Eight Sages,’ its thesis holding that withdrawal was superior and service inferior, which he showed Sun Chuo.
translations.idiomatic: He wrote the ‘Eight Sages’ essay favoring reclusion over office and showed it to Sun Chuo.

sentences.zh: 綽與往反，以體公識遠者則出處同歸。

translations.literal: Chuo debated back and forth, holding that those who embody the public good and see far find withdrawal and service return to the same end.
translations.idiomatic: Chuo answered that the far-sighted serve or hide to the same moral end.

sentences.zh: 嘗與蔡系送客於征虜亭，與系爭言。

translations.literal: He once saw off a guest with Cai Xi at the General Who Conquers the Barbarians pavilion and quarreled in debate with Xi.
translations.idiomatic: Once he argued with Cai Xi at the conquest-general’s pavilion.

sentences.zh: 系推萬落床，冠帽傾脫。

translations.literal: Xi pushed Wan off the couch; cap and headcloth slipped awry.
translations.idiomatic: Cai Xi tipped him off the bench and knocked his cap askew.

sentences.zh: 萬徐拂衣就席，神意自若，坐定，謂系曰：「卿幾壞我面。

translations.literal: Wan slowly brushed his robes and took his seat, spirit and expression calm as before; when seated he said to Xi: “You nearly ruined my face.”
translations.idiomatic: Wan dusted off, sat down, and said, ‘You nearly ruined my face.’

sentences.zh: 」系曰：「本不為卿面計。

translations.literal: Xi said: “I never calculated for your face’s sake.”
translations.idiomatic: Xi shot back, ‘I was not thinking of your face.’

sentences.zh: 」然俱不以介意，時亦以此稱之。

translations.literal: Yet neither minded; contemporaries also praised this.
translations.idiomatic: Neither cared; onlookers admired the poise.

sentences.zh: 弱冠，辟司徒掾，遷右西屬，不就。

translations.literal: At his capping he was summoned as a clerk to the Minister of Education; promoted to Western Bureau subordinate, he did not take office.
translations.idiomatic: He was called to the minister of education’s staff and a western bureau post—he declined.

sentences.zh: 簡文帝作相，聞其名，召為撫軍從事中郎。

translations.literal: When Emperor Jianwen was chief minister, hearing his fame, he summoned him as aide to the General Who Pacifies the Army.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Jianwen heard of him and named him aide to the pacification general.

sentences.zh: 萬著白綸巾，鶴氅裘，履版而前。

translations.literal: Wan wore a white gauze kerchief, crane-feather cloak, and clogs as he advanced.
translations.idiomatic: He arrived in white silk cap, crane cloak, and wooden clogs.

sentences.zh: 既見，與帝共談移日。

translations.literal: After the audience he conversed with the emperor until the day turned.
translations.idiomatic: They talked the day away.

sentences.zh: 太原王述，萬之妻父也，為揚州刺史。

translations.literal: Wang Shu of Taiyuan, Wan’s father-in-law, was Governor of Yangzhou.
translations.idiomatic: His father-in-law Wang Shu governed Yangzhou.

sentences.zh: 萬嘗衣白綸巾，乘平肩輿，徑至聽事前，謂述曰：「人言君侯癡，君侯信自癡。

translations.literal: Wan once wore a white gauze kerchief, rode an open palanquin, and went straight to the main hall, saying to Shu: “People say you, lord, are foolish—you truly are foolish yourself.”
translations.idiomatic: He once rode straight into Wang Shu’s hall in white cap and said, ‘They call you a fool—you really are one.’

sentences.zh: 」述曰：「非無此論，但晚合耳。

translations.literal: Shu said: “It is not that such talk does not exist—only it fits late.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Shu answered, ‘The rumor exists—I am just a slow starter.’

sentences.zh: 」萬再遷豫州刺史、領淮南太守、監司豫冀並四州軍事、假節。

translations.literal: Wan was twice promoted to Governor of Yuzhou, concurrently Prefect of Huainan, overseer of military affairs in Si, Yu, Ji, and Bing four provinces, with credential staff.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to Yuzhou governor, Huainan prefect, and commander of four provinces with the staff.

sentences.zh: 王羲之與桓溫箋曰：「謝萬才流經通，處廊廟，參諷議，故是後來一器。

translations.literal: Wang Xizhi wrote in a note to Huan Wen: “Xie Wan’s talent flows broadly; placed in the court hall to join counsel, he is indeed a vessel of the later generation.”
translations.idiomatic: Wang Xizhi told Huan Wen, ‘Wan belongs in council, not the frontier.’

sentences.zh: 而今屈其邁往之氣，以俯順荒餘，近是違才易務矣。

translations.literal: “Now to bend his soaring spirit to submit to wasteland remnants is nearly to violate talent and swap tasks.”
translations.idiomatic: ‘Sending his dash to herd ruins misuses him.’

sentences.zh: 」溫不從。

translations.literal: Wen did not follow.
translations.idiomatic: Huan Wen ignored the advice.

sentences.zh: 萬既受任北征，矜豪傲物，嘗以嘯詠自高，未嘗撫眾。

translations.literal: Wan, having received appointment for the northern expedition, was arrogant and disdainful of others; he often elevated himself with whistling and chanting, never comforting the troops.
translations.idiomatic: Wan took command preening on verse and whistle, never visiting the ranks.

sentences.zh: 兄安深憂之，自隊主將帥已下，安無不慰勉。

translations.literal: His elder brother An deeply worried; from team leaders and commanders downward, An had no one whom he did not console and encourage.
translations.idiomatic: An personally encouraged every officer down to team leaders.

sentences.zh: 謂萬曰：「汝為元帥，諸將宜數接對，以悅其心，豈有傲誕若斯而能濟事也！

translations.literal: He told Wan: “You are commander-in-chief; the generals ought to be met frequently to please their hearts—how can arrogance and eccentricity like this accomplish anything!”
translations.idiomatic: An warned, ‘A commander must court his generals—swagger wins nothing.’

sentences.zh: 」萬乃召集諸將，都無所說，直以如意指四坐云：「諸將皆勁卒。

translations.literal: Wan thereupon assembled the generals, said nothing at all, merely pointed with a ruyi around the seats, saying: “You generals are all crack troops.”
translations.idiomatic: Wan called a meeting, said nothing useful, and flicked his ruyi at them: ‘Fine soldiers, all of you.’

sentences.zh: 」諸將益恨之。

translations.literal: The generals hated him all the more.
translations.idiomatic: The officers seethed.

sentences.zh: 既而先遣征虜將軍劉建修治馬頭城池，自率眾入渦潁，以援洛陽。

translations.literal: Presently he first sent Liu Jian, General Who Conquers the Barbarians, to repair Makou fortress, then led the host into Guo and Ying to relieve Luoyang.
translations.idiomatic: He sent Liu Jian to repair Makou, then marched toward Guo–Ying to relieve Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 北中郎將郗曇以疾病退還彭城，萬以為賊盛致退，便引軍還，眾遂潰散，狼狽單歸，廢為庶人。

translations.literal: Xi Tan, General of the Centre of the North, because of illness withdrew to Pengcheng; Wan thought the enemy strong had caused the retreat and thereupon led the army back; the host thereupon scattered in rout; he fled alone in disgrace and was degraded to commoner.
translations.idiomatic: When Xi Tan fell back ill, Wan assumed a rout and ran—his army collapsed and he was stripped to commoner status.

sentences.zh: 後復以為散騎常侍，會卒，時年四十二，因以為贈。

translations.literal: Later he was again appointed Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary; he happened to die, aged forty-two; therefore that posthumous gift was granted.
translations.idiomatic: Recalled as cavalier attendant, he died at forty-two; that title became his posthumous honor.

sentences.zh: =萬子 韶=

translations.literal: Equals signs framing the subheading ‘Wan’s son: Shao’ in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: Wan’s son: Shao

sentences.zh: 子韶，字穆度，少有名。

translations.literal: His son Shao, courtesy name Madu, from youth had reputation.
translations.idiomatic: Shao, courtesy Madu, was known young.

sentences.zh: 時謝氏憂彥秀者，稱封、胡、羯、末。

translations.literal: At that time among the Xies those worried over as ‘fine shoots’ were called Feng, Hu, Jie, Mo.
translations.idiomatic: The clan’s brightest youths were nicknamed Feng, Hu, Jie, Mo.

sentences.zh: 封謂韶，胡謂主朗，羯謂玄，末謂川，皆其小字也。

translations.literal: Feng meant Shao, Hu meant Lang, Jie meant Xuan, Mo meant Chuan—all were childhood names.
translations.idiomatic: Feng was Shao, Hu Lang, Jie Xuan, Mo Chuan—baby names all.

sentences.zh: 韶、朗、川並早卒，惟玄以功名終，韶至車騎司馬。

translations.literal: Shao, Lang, and Chuan all died young; only Xuan ended with merit and fame; Shao reached Marshal of Chariots and Cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: Shao, Lang, and Chuan died young; only Xuan lived to glory; Shao rose to marshal of cavalry.

sentences.zh: 韶子恩，字景伯，宏達有遠略，韶為黃門郎、武昌太守。

translations.literal: Shao’s son En, courtesy name Jingbo, was magnanimous and farsighted; Shao served as Palace Attendant and Prefect of Wuchang.
translations.idiomatic: En, courtesy Jingbo, was broad-gauged; Shao had been palace attendant and Wuchang prefect.

sentences.zh: 恩三子、曜、弘微，皆曆顯位。

translations.literal: En had three sons; Yao and Hongwei among them all held prominent posts.
translations.idiomatic: His boys Yao and Hongwei each climbed to high office.

sentences.zh: =安兄據子 朗=

translations.literal: Equals signs framing the subheading ‘An’s elder brother Ju’s son: Lang’ in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: Son of An’s brother Ju: Lang

sentences.zh: 朗字長度。

translations.literal: Lang, courtesy name Changdu.
translations.idiomatic: Lang’s courtesy name was Changdu.

sentences.zh: 父據，早卒。

translations.literal: His father Ju died early.
translations.idiomatic: Father Ju died young.

sentences.zh: 朗善言玄理，文義豔發，名亞于玄。

translations.literal: Lang was skilled in discussing arcane principles; his writings blazed with color; his name stood second to Xuan’s.
translations.idiomatic: Lang’s metaphysics and prose rivaled Xuan’s.

sentences.zh: 總角時，病新起，體甚贏，未堪勞，于叔父安前與沙門支遁朗論，遂至相苦。

translations.literal: When still a boy, recovering from illness, his body was very frail, unable to bear exertion; before his uncle An he debated abstruse points with the monk Zhidun until they grew sharp with each other.
translations.idiomatic: Still weak from illness, he debated Zhidun before An until sparks flew.

sentences.zh: 其母王氏再遣信令還，安欲留，使竟論，王氏因出云：「新婦少遭艱難，一生所寄惟在此兒。

translations.literal: His mother Lady Wang twice sent messengers ordering him home; An wished to keep him and let the debate finish; Lady Wang therefore came out and said: “Your new daughter-in-law met hardship young; all my life leans on this boy.”
translations.idiomatic: His mother dragged him away, crying that her life hung on this frail son.

sentences.zh: 」遂流涕攜朗去。

translations.literal: Thereupon weeping, she led Lang away.
translations.idiomatic: Weeping, she took him home.

sentences.zh: 安謂坐客曰：「家嫂辭情慷慨，恨不使朝士見之。

translations.literal: An told the seated guests: “My sister-in-law’s words are stirring—I regret the court gentlemen could not see them.”
translations.idiomatic: An told guests, ‘My sister-in-law’s speech would shame the capital.’

sentences.zh: 」朗終於東陽太守。

translations.literal: Lang ended his days as Prefect of Dongyang.
translations.idiomatic: He died as Dongyang prefect.

sentences.zh: 朗子 重

translations.literal: Lang’s son: Chong.
translations.idiomatic: Lang’s son: Chong

sentences.zh: 子重，字景重，明秀有才名，為會稽王道子驃騎長史。

translations.literal: His son Chong, courtesy name Jingzhong, was bright and talented, famed for ability; he was chief clerk to Prince Daozi of Kuaiji’s general of agile cavalry.
translations.idiomatic: Chong, courtesy Jingzhong, shone as chief clerk to Daozi’s agile cavalry command.

sentences.zh: 嘗因侍坐，于時月夜明淨，道子歎以為佳。

translations.literal: Once while attending in service, under a moonlit night clear and bright, Daozi sighed that it was fine.
translations.idiomatic: Once on a clear moonlit night Daozi sighed at the beauty.

sentences.zh: 重率爾曰：「意謂乃不如微雲點綴。

translations.literal: Chong bluntly said: “My thought is that it is not as good as a slight tracing of clouds.”
translations.idiomatic: Chong said he preferred a wisp of cloud.

sentences.zh: 」道子因戲重曰：「卿居心不淨，乃復強欲滓穢太清邪！」

translations.literal: Daozi therefore teased Chong: “Your mind is not pure—do you still wish to muddy the Great Purity!”
translations.idiomatic: Daozi joked, ‘Impure heart—you would stain the empyrean!’

translations.literal: An equals sign printed alone in the received text as a layout divider.

sentences.zh: 重子 絢

translations.literal: Chong’s son: Xuan.
translations.idiomatic: Chong’s son: Xuan

translations.literal: An equals sign printed alone in the received text as a layout divider.

sentences.zh: 子絢，字宣映，曾於公坐戲調，無禮于其舅袁湛。

translations.literal: His son Xuan, courtesy name Xuanying, once in public seating jested offensively and was rude to his maternal uncle Yuan Zhan.
translations.idiomatic: Xuan, courtesy Xuanying, once insulted uncle Yuan Zhan at a gathering.

sentences.zh: 湛甚不堪之，謂曰：「汝父昔已輕舅，汝今復來加我，可謂世無渭陽情也。

translations.literal: Zhan could hardly bear it and said: “Your father already slighted his uncle; you now come again to add to me—one may say the world lacks the affection of the Wei-yang.”
translations.idiomatic: Zhan snapped, ‘Your father insulted me; you continue it—kinship means nothing in your house.’

sentences.zh: 」絢父重，即王胡之外孫，與舅亦有不協之論，湛故有此及雲。

translations.literal: Chong’s father was the maternal grandson of Wang Hu; he too had words of discord with his uncle; hence Zhan referred to this.
translations.idiomatic: Chong, Wang Hu’s grandson, had quarreled with his uncle—Zhan remembered.

sentences.zh: 安弟 石

translations.literal: An’s younger brother: Shi.
translations.idiomatic: An’s brother: Shi

sentences.zh: 石字石奴。

translations.literal: Shi, courtesy name Shinu.
translations.idiomatic: Shi, courtesy Shinu.

sentences.zh: 初拜秘書郎，累遷尚書僕射。

translations.literal: At first appointed Palace Secretary, by stages promoted to Vice Director of the Imperial Secretariat.
translations.idiomatic: He rose from palace secretary to vice director.

sentences.zh: 征句難，以勳封興平縣伯。

translations.literal: He campaigned against Gou Nan and by merit was enfeoffed as Baron of Xingping.
translations.idiomatic: The Gou Nan campaign won him the Xingping barony.

sentences.zh: 淮肥之役，詔石解僕射，以將軍假節征討大都督，與兄子玄、琰破苻堅。

translations.literal: In the Huai–Fei campaign, an edict ordered Shi to relinquish the vice directorship, and as general with credential staff and grand commander for conquest, together with his elder brother’s sons Xuan and Yan, he defeated Fu Jian.
translations.idiomatic: At Fei River he shed the vice director’s tile, took the grand command, and broke Fu Jian with Xuan and Yan.

sentences.zh: 先是，童謠云：「誰謂爾堅石打碎。

translations.literal: Earlier, a children’s rhyme said: “Who calls you hard? Stone smashes you.”
translations.idiomatic: A children’s rhyme ran, ‘Who says you’re hard as stone? Stone shatters you.’

sentences.zh: 」故桓豁皆以「石」名子，以邀功焉。

translations.literal: Therefore Huan Huo all named sons ‘Shi’ to invite the merit.
translations.idiomatic: So Huan Huo named sons ‘Stone’ to claim the omen.

sentences.zh: 堅之敗也，雖功始牢之，而成于玄、琰，然石時實為都督焉。

translations.literal: In Jian’s defeat, though the merit began with Laozhi, it was completed by Xuan and Yan, yet Shi at the time was truly the overall commander.
translations.idiomatic: Laozhi opened the victory, Xuan and Yan finished it—but Shi held supreme command.

sentences.zh: 遷中軍將軍、尚書令，更封南康郡公。

translations.literal: He was promoted to General of the Central Army and Director of the Imperial Secretariat, and his fief was changed to Duke of Nankang commandery.
translations.idiomatic: He took the central army, the secretariat, and a Nankang ducal title.

sentences.zh: 于時學校陵遲，石上疏請興復國學，以訓胄子，班下州郡，普修鄉校。

translations.literal: At that time schools were in decay; Shi submitted a memorial asking to revive the national academy to instruct noble sons, promulgated the order to prefectures and commanderies, and broadly restored village schools.
translations.idiomatic: He memorialized to rebuild the imperial academy and local schools across the realm.

sentences.zh: 疏奏，孝武帝納焉。

translations.literal: When the memorial was presented, Emperor Xiaowu accepted it.
translations.idiomatic: Emperor Xiaowu approved.

sentences.zh: 兄安薨，石遷衛將軍，加散騎常侍。

translations.literal: When elder brother An died, Shi was promoted to General Who Guards the Court with additional Cavalier Attendant-in-Ordinary.
translations.idiomatic: An’s death moved him up to General Who Guards the Court with cavalier rank.

sentences.zh: 以公事與吏部郎王恭互相短長，恭甚忿恨，自陳褊厄不允，且疾源深固，乞還私門。

translations.literal: Over public business he traded barbs with Wang Gong of the Ministry of Personnel; Gong was furious, stating himself cramped and obstructed, with illness deep-rooted, and begged to return to private life.
translations.idiomatic: He feuded with Wang Gong of personnel; Gong quit in fury, pleading illness.

sentences.zh: 石亦上疏遜位。

translations.literal: Shi also submitted a memorial yielding office.
translations.idiomatic: Shi offered his own resignation.

sentences.zh: 有司奏，石輒去職，免官。

translations.literal: The relevant officials reported that Shi had abruptly left duty; he was dismissed from office.
translations.idiomatic: The ministry ruled he had abandoned post and stripped him.

sentences.zh: 詔曰：「石以疾求退，豈准之常制！

translations.literal: An edict said: “Shi because of illness seeks retirement—how can that match the constant statute!”
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, ‘Illness is no ordinary reason to quit!’

sentences.zh: 其喻令還。

translations.literal: Order him to understand and return.
translations.idiomatic: Tell him to come back.

sentences.zh: 」歲餘不起。

translations.literal: For more than a year he did not rise to serve.
translations.idiomatic: He stayed home over a year.

sentences.zh: 表十餘上，帝不許。

translations.literal: He submitted more than ten memorials; the emperor did not permit.
translations.idiomatic: Ten-plus pleas went unanswered.

sentences.zh: 石乞依故尚書令王彪之例，於府綜攝，詔聽之。

translations.literal: Shi begged to follow the precedent of former Director Wang Biaozhi, managing affairs from his mansion; an edict granted it.
translations.idiomatic: He won permission to run the secretariat from home like Wang Biaozhi.

sentences.zh: 疾篤，進位開府儀同三司，加鼓吹，未拜，卒，時年六十二。

translations.literal: When his illness was grave, he was advanced to an office ceremonially equal to the Three Excellencies with a military band; before investiture he died, aged sixty-two.
translations.idiomatic: They offered him opentent rank and musicians; he died at sixty-two before the ceremony.

sentences.zh: 石少患-{面}-創，療之莫愈，乃自匿。

translations.literal: From youth Shi suffered facial sores; treatment never cured them, so he hid them.
translations.idiomatic: A chronic facial ulcer drove him to hide his face.

sentences.zh: 夜有物來舐其瘡，隨舐隨差，舐處甚白，故世呼為「謝白-{面}-」。

translations.literal: At night a creature came and licked the sores; as it licked they healed; where licked the skin was very white—hence the world called him ‘Xie White-Face.’
translations.idiomatic: Something licked the wound white by night—folk dubbed him ‘Pale-Face Xie.’

sentences.zh: 石在職務存文刻，既無他才望，直以宰相弟兼有大才，遂居清顯，而聚斂無饜，取譏當世。

translations.literal: Shi in office pursued punctilious paperwork; lacking other talent or prestige, he simply relied on being a prime minister’s younger brother and having a great name, and thus occupied a pure, eminent post, yet amassed wealth insatiably, earning ridicule in his age.
translations.idiomatic: He rose on his brother’s name, nitpicked documents, and hoarded wealth—contemporaries sneered.

sentences.zh: 追贈司空，禮官議諡，博士范弘之議諡曰襄墨公，語在弘之傳。

translations.literal: Posthumously he was awarded Minister of Works; ritual officials debated his posthumous title; erudite Fan Hongzhi proposed ‘Duke Xiangmo’—the language is in Hongzhi’s biography.
translations.idiomatic: Fan Hongzhi wanted the harsh epithet Xiangmo; his memorial survives elsewhere.

sentences.zh: 朝議不從，單諡曰襄。

translations.literal: Court debate did not follow; he received only the posthumous title ‘Xiang.’
translations.idiomatic: The court settled on ‘Xiang’ alone.

sentences.zh: 子汪嗣，早卒。

translations.literal: His son Wang succeeded; he died young.
translations.idiomatic: Son Wang inherited and died young.

sentences.zh: 汪從兄-{沖}-以子明慧嗣，為孫恩所害。

translations.literal: Wang’s cousin Chong used his son Minghui to continue the line; [Minghui] was killed by Sun En.
translations.idiomatic: Cousin Chong adopted heir Minghui, whom Sun En murdered.

sentences.zh: 明慧從兄喻復以子暠嗣。

translations.literal: Minghui’s cousin Yu again used his son Gao to succeed.
translations.idiomatic: Yu then installed son Gao as heir.

sentences.zh: 宋受禪，國除。

translations.literal: When Song received the abdication, the state was abolished.
translations.idiomatic: The Liu-Song founding ended the fief.

sentences.zh: =從子 邈=

translations.literal: Equals signs framing the subheading ‘Nephew: Miao’ in the received text.
translations.idiomatic: Nephew: Miao

sentences.zh: 邈字茂度。

translations.literal: Miao, courtesy name Maodu.
translations.idiomatic: Miao, courtesy Maodu.

sentences.zh: 父鐵，永嘉太守。

translations.literal: His father Tie was Prefect of Yongjia.
translations.idiomatic: Father Tie governed Yongjia.

sentences.zh: 邈性剛鯁，無所屈撓，頗有理識。

translations.literal: Miao by nature was stubbornly upright, yielding to nothing, and had considerable judgment.
translations.idiomatic: He was rigid, fearless, and shrewd.

sentences.zh: 累遷侍中。

translations.literal: By stages he was promoted to Palace Attendant.
translations.idiomatic: He rose to palace attendant.

sentences.zh: 時孝武帝觴樂之後多賜侍臣文詔，辭義有不雅者，邈輒焚毀之，其他侍臣被詔者或宣揚之，故論者以此多邈。

translations.literal: At that time after Emperor Xiaowu’s drinking and music he often gifted literary edicts to attending ministers; when the wording was inelegant, Miao always burned them; other attendants who received edicts sometimes publicized them—therefore debaters on this account praised Miao.
translations.idiomatic: After imperial banquets Xiaowu handed out draft edicts; Miao burned the bad ones while others flaunted theirs—critics preferred Miao’s discretion.

sentences.zh: 後為吳興太守。

translations.literal: Later he became Prefect of Wuxing.
translations.idiomatic: He later governed Wuxing.

sentences.zh: 孫恩之亂，為賊胡桀、郜驃等所執，害之。

translations.literal: During Sun En’s rebellion he was seized by the bandits Hu Jie, Gao Piao, and others and killed.
translations.idiomatic: Sun En’s men, Hu Jie and Gao Piao among them, took him and killed him.

sentences.zh: 賊逼令北面，邈厲聲曰：「我不得罪天子，何北面之有！

translations.literal: The bandits forced him to face north; Miao said in a stern voice: “I have not offended the Son of Heaven—why should I face north!”
translations.idiomatic: They ordered him to bow north; he shouted, ‘I wronged no emperor—I face no usurper!’

sentences.zh: 」遂害之。

translations.literal: Thereupon they killed him.
translations.idiomatic: They cut him down.

sentences.zh: 邈妻郗氏，甚妒。

translations.literal: Miao’s wife was of the Xi clan and was very jealous.
translations.idiomatic: Lady Xi, his wife, was fiercely jealous.

sentences.zh: 邈先娶妾，郗氏怨懟，與邈書告絕。

translations.literal: Miao had earlier taken a concubine; Lady Xi resented it and sent Miao a letter severing ties.
translations.idiomatic: She repudiated him in writing when he took a concubine.

sentences.zh: 邈以其書非婦人詞，疑其門下生仇玄達為之作，遂斥玄達。

translations.literal: Miao, because the letter was not in a woman’s phrasing, suspected his student Qiu Xuanda had written it for her and dismissed Xuanda.
translations.idiomatic: He thought student Qiu Xuanda forged her voice and expelled him.

sentences.zh: 玄達怒，遂投孫恩，並害邈兄弟，竟至滅門。

translations.literal: Xuanda in anger thereupon joined Sun En and together killed Miao’s brothers, reaching extinction of the whole household.
translations.idiomatic: Qiu fled to Sun En and helped wipe out Miao’s kin.

sentences.zh: 【史論】==史臣曰：建元之後，時政多虞，巨猾陸梁，權臣橫恣。

translations.literal: 【Historical essay】==The historians say: After Jianyuan, the times held many alarms; great villains rampaged and powerful ministers acted willfully.
translations.idiomatic: The historians write: After Jianyuan, traitors and strongmen ran wild.

sentences.zh: 其有兼將相於中外，系存亡於社稷，負扆資之以端拱，鑿井賴之以晏安者，其惟謝氏乎！

translations.literal: Those who combined general and minister inside and outside, on whom the altars’ survival hung, whom the ruler leaning on the screen relied on to govern with folded hands, and on whom digging wells depended for peace—was that not the Xie clan!
translations.idiomatic: Who held both sword and seal, steadied the throne, and let the court breathe easy? The Xies.

sentences.zh: 簡侯任總中台，效彰分閫；

translations.literal: Marquis Jian held the central terrace in charge; his merit shone in separate commands.
translations.idiomatic: Marquis Jian ran the center and the frontier alike.

sentences.zh: 正議雲唱，喪禮墮而復弘；

translations.literal: With upright discourse like clouds, collapsed mourning rites were enlarged again.
translations.idiomatic: His principled voice restored ritual when mourning law frayed.

sentences.zh: 遺音既補，雅樂缺而還備。

translations.literal: Once the lost tones were mended, court music—though wanting—returned complete.
translations.idiomatic: He refitted bells and stones so the court heard music again.

sentences.zh: 君子哉，斯人也！

translations.literal: A gentleman—such was this man!
translations.idiomatic: A gentleman, that man.

sentences.zh: 文靖始居塵外，高謝人間，嘯詠山林，浮泛江海，當此之時，蕭然有陵霞之致。

translations.literal: Wenjing first dwelt beyond the dust, loftily quitting the human world, whistling and chanting in mountains and forests, drifting on rivers and seas; at that time he had an air as if he would mount the rosy clouds.
translations.idiomatic: Xie An began above the fray, singing in hills and on rivers like an immortal.

sentences.zh: 暨於褫薜蘿而襲硃組，去衡泌而踐丹墀，庶績於是用康，彝倫以之載穆。

translations.literal: When he cast off rushes and vines to don crimson cords, left the humble gate to tread the vermillion steps, myriad tasks thereupon were ordered and human relations thereby grew harmonious.
translations.idiomatic: Once he took office, the realm steadied and ethics calmed.

sentences.zh: 苻堅百萬之眾已瞰吳江，桓溫九五之心將移晉鼎，衣冠易慮，遠邇崩心。

translations.literal: Fu Jian’s million already glared across the Wu River; Huan Wen’s heart of the ‘nine-five’ would shift the Jin cauldron; caps and gowns changed their minds; far and near hearts collapsed.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Jian’s horde and Huan Wen’s ambition terrified every minister.

sentences.zh: 從容而杜奸謀，宴衎而清群寇，宸居獲太山之固，惟揚去累卵之危，斯為盛矣。

translations.literal: With ease he blocked treasonous plots; feasting, he cleared the mass of bandits—the imperial seat gained Mount Tai’s solidity, only Yangzhou shed the peril of stacked eggs—this was greatness indeed.
translations.idiomatic: He broke plots over wine and saved Jin from stacked odds—true greatness.

sentences.zh: 然激繁會於期服之辰，敦一歡于百金之費，廢禮于偷薄之俗，崇侈于耕戰之秋，雖欲混哀樂而同歸，齊奢儉於一致，而不知頹風已扇，雅道日淪，國之儀刑，豈期若是！

translations.literal: Yet he stirred elaborate gatherings in the heart of hemp mourning, pressed one pleasure at the cost of a hundred in gold, abandoned ritual amid a callous age, and exalted extravagance in a season of plow and war—though wishing to blend grief and joy in one return and equalize luxury and thrift, he did not know the falling wind already fanned, the correct way daily sank, and could the state’s model expect to be thus!
translations.idiomatic: Yet music during mourning and feasts of gold eroded the very manners he saved—decay spread unseen.

sentences.zh: 琰稱貞幹，卒以忠勇垂名；

translations.literal: Yan was called chaste and competent, ending with a name for loyalty and courage;
translations.idiomatic: Yan: integrity and courage;

sentences.zh: 混曰風流，竟以文詞獲譽：並階時宰，無墮家風。

translations.literal: Hun was styled elegant, ending with praise for literary words: both ascended with the age’s ministers, not disgracing the family tone.
translations.idiomatic: Hun: poetry and polish—both kept the clan’s stature.

sentences.zh: 奕萬以放肆為高，石奴以褊濁興累，雖曰微纇，猶稱名實。

translations.literal: Yi and Wan took wantonness as high; Shinu brought trouble through pettiness and turbidity; though called minor flaws, name and reality were still weighed.
translations.idiomatic: Yi and Wan flaunted excess; Shi’s meanness stained them—small faults, true labels.

sentences.zh: 康樂才兼文武，志存匡濟，淮肥之役，勍寇望之而土崩；

translations.literal: Kangle united civil and military talent, his aim set on aiding the age; in the Huai–Fei campaign, fierce foes saw him and crumbled;
translations.idiomatic: Kangle—Xie Xuan—was soldier and scholar; at Fei River enemies shattered at his name;

sentences.zh: 渦潁之師，中州應之而席捲。

translations.literal: on the Guo–Ying expedition, the central plains answered and were swept away.
translations.idiomatic: his Guo–Ying thrust rolled up the heartland.

sentences.zh: 方欲西平鞏洛，北定幽燕，廟算有遺，良圖不果，降齡何促，功敗垂成，拊其遺文，經綸遠矣。

translations.literal: Just as he wished to pacify Gong and Luo on the west and settle You and Yan on the north, planning fell short and fine designs did not bear fruit—how brief his years, merit failing on the verge of completion; stroking his surviving writings, his ordering of the realm reaches far.
translations.idiomatic: He nearly reconquered the north—cut down young, his plans live on in his words.

sentences.zh: 贊曰：安西英爽，才兼辯博。

translations.literal: The eulogy says: The Marquis of the West, bright and keen, united talent with eloquence and breadth.
translations.idiomatic: The eulogy praises the marquis of the west, brilliant and learned.

sentences.zh: 宣力方鎮，流聲台閣。

translations.literal: He labored in the provinces, his voice flowed through the halls.
translations.idiomatic: He spent his strength on the frontier and left his name in the capital.

sentences.zh: 太保沈浮，曠若虛舟。

translations.literal: The Grand Tutor floated through the world, broad as an empty boat.
translations.idiomatic: The grand tutor moved through office like a raft on an empty stream.

sentences.zh: 任高百辟，情惟一丘。

translations.literal: Duty towered over the hundred officials; his heart clung to one hill.
translations.idiomatic: Rank towered above his peers, yet one hill held all his longing.

sentences.zh: 琰邈忠壯，奕萬虛放。

translations.literal: Yan and Miao, loyal and bold; Yi and Wan, hollow and wild.
translations.idiomatic: Yan and Miao embody loyalty; Yi and Wan embody unbridled ease.

sentences.zh: 為龍為光，或卿或將。

translations.literal: As dragons, as glory—minister or general.
translations.idiomatic: They were dragons, they brought glory—some as ministers, some as generals.

sentences.zh: 偉哉獻武，功宣授斧。

translations.literal: How great Xianwu, merit fit for the axe of command!
translations.idiomatic: How great Xianwu, whose merit earned the battle-axe of command.

sentences.zh: 克翦凶渠，幾清中宇。

translations.literal: He could have scoured the villains and nearly cleared the central realm.
translations.idiomatic: He nearly scoured the realm clean of rebels.
